title: Long AMD — AI Chip Supercycle FOMC Dip Entry
entry: Enter $525-550 (AMD closed at an all-time high of $547.26 on June 15; a FOMC-driven 2-4% pullback on June 16-17 creates the entry). If no pullback materializes, enter $540-548 at market with a smaller initial tranche (50% of target size). Scale: 60% on first entry; 40% add if AMD dips to $525-535 on Warsh hawkish shock. Do NOT add below $510.
stop_loss: $495 daily close (~9.2% below $545 midpoint) — implies AMD misses Q3 guidance on MI300 supply constraints, OR Warsh hike drives a broad 10%+ tech-sector correction, OR NVDA announces Blackwell Ultra production ramp that eliminates AMD's wait-list premium
targets: $590 — AMD Q3 2026 data center revenue guidance raised above $7B; hyperscaler allocations confirm AMD market share gains in AI accelerator segment; +8.3% from $545 midpoint
$640 — AMD MI400 roadmap announced with named hyperscaler design wins at Hot Chips conference (August 2026); AMD trades to premium on forward data center GPU guidance; +17.4%
$720 — AMD captures 20%+ AI GPU market share; Q3 2026 earnings beat with data center +80% YoY continues; AMD re-rates from 'catching up' to 'co-leader' status; +32.1%
catalyst: AMD closed at an all-time high of $547.26 on June 15, 2026. Q1 2026 data center segment revenue was $5.8 billion (up 57% YoY), driven by AMD Instinct GPU shipments (MI300 series), with named hyperscaler deployments confirmed at Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle. AMD guided Q2 2026 total revenue at approximately $11.2 billion — implying data center revenue of $6.5-7B, a continued acceleration. The broader AI capex supercycle was confirmed this week by NVIDIA's $25B bond sale attracting $85B in orders (3.4x oversubscribed), demonstrating insatiable hyperscaler AI spending. AMD stock surged 16% on Q1 2026 earnings (May 5) and has continued making new all-time highs into the FOMC.
thesis:
AMD's Q1 2026 data center revenue of $5.8B — up 57% YoY — validates that AMD is not merely a runner-up to NVIDIA but a genuine dual-supplier for hyperscaler AI workloads. The hyperscaler procurement calculus is structural: Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle cannot have 100% NVDA exposure without supply-chain vulnerability. AMD's MI300 series provides the only competitive alternative at scale for AI training and inference at the 192GB HBM3 memory density that large transformer models require. The 57% data center growth rate, sustained for multiple consecutive quarters, shows AMD is gaining share — not just riding the market's overall growth.

NVDA's own market dynamics create AMD tailwind. NVIDIA's $25B bond at 3.4x oversubscription signals that AI infrastructure investment is so capital-intensive and time-sensitive that hyperscalers are willing to overpay for secured supply. Any NVDA supply constraint — Blackwell ramp delays, CoWoS packaging capacity limitations at TSMC — increases AMD MI300 order flow. AMD's Q2 guidance of $11.2B implies data center acceleration continues, with MI400 ramp beginning H2 2026 creating a forward catalyst. The Hot Chips conference (August) is the first public venue where AMD is expected to preview MI400 specifications — a catalyst within the 6-10 week position horizon and before Q3 earnings.

The FOMC context creates the entry opportunity specifically. Warsh's June 17 press conference introduces 2-4% intraday volatility for high-multiple tech stocks — AMD at approximately 47x forward earnings is sensitive to rate-hike signals. If Warsh is hawkish, AMD may pull back 3-5% from $547 to $520-535, creating a dip entry into a confirmed multi-quarter revenue ramp. The thesis does not depend on FOMC being dovish: it depends on AI capex being real (confirmed by NVDA bond demand), AMD MI300 execution being on track (confirmed Q1), and the MI400 roadmap creating forward momentum (August Hot Chips). A FOMC-driven pullback to $525-535 is a gift entry at better-than-today prices.

The counter-party is the NVDA bull who argues AMD cannot meaningfully close the gap on NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem — that hardware parity is irrelevant without the 10-year developer moat NVIDIA has built. This is the most serious bear argument: enterprise AI developers default to CUDA, and AMD's ROCm software stack requires active porting effort that most teams avoid. The bull rebuttal is that hyperscalers (Microsoft, Meta, Oracle) have the engineering resources to maintain both software stacks and they actively fund AMD software work — the enterprise CUDA lock-in is real but does not apply to the 5-10 hyperscalers who dominate 60% of AI GPU purchasing.
bull_case: AMD Q3 2026 data center guidance raised to $7B+ on Q2 earnings (late July); MI400 receives first hyperscaler design wins announced at Hot Chips (August). NVDA supply constraints on Blackwell B200 push incremental orders to AMD. AMD to $590 (Target 1) by late July, $640 (Target 2) by September. Tail: AMD announces a major AI software stack acquisition that re-rates the business toward $800 as the CUDA software moat concern is addressed directly.
bear_case: Warsh hikes 25bps and signals July follow-through; broad tech sector correction of 8-12%; AMD falls from $547 to $495-510. AMD Q2 earnings (late July) miss on data center revenue ($5.5B vs. $6.5B-7B guidance) due to CoWoS packaging constraints at TSMC limiting MI300 shipments. Stop at $495 triggered. Tail: NVDA announces Blackwell Ultra at 35% lower per-FLOP cost, directly reducing AMD's competitive positioning.
invalidation: $495 daily close, OR AMD Q2 data center revenue below $5.5B (guidance miss of >15%), OR NVDA announces Blackwell Ultra production ramp eliminating AMD wait-list premium, OR Warsh rate hike triggers 10%+ tech sector correction

outcome.outcome_label: Stop hit at $495 — AMD closed $494.95 on July 28
outcome.note: AMD fell -5.17% on July 28 to $494.95, breaching the $495 daily-close stop. The NVDA circular financing narrative ($250B OpenAI backstop, confirmed WSJ/Bloomberg July 27) repriced hyperscaler AI capex ROI sector-wide. The July 28 Asia chip rout (KOSPI -10.8%, SK Hynix -14.7%, ASML -8.4% on China DUV mass production) cascaded into US semis. The AI GPU supercycle thesis is structurally challenged by circular financing opacity; AMD MI400 roadmap (August Hot Chips) remains a potential re-entry catalyst if circular financing narrative resolves.
